lines.trans: Report, Tariq! Which room keys got mixed up during the noon telephone call?
Look at my paper book: two young hikers booked Room Two on the first floor.
Yes, lovely polite hikers—and a quiet lady with a floral hatbox booked Room Six!
Now tell Nour where your glasses were when you handed out tags Two and Six.
Oh dear... upside down, two becomes five, no—two and six look remarkably similar blurry!
Did the hikers take backpacks to Room Six while the hatbox went to Room Two?!
Lucky for you, boss, both guests dropped their bags outside the doors and went for lunch!
Really?! Neither guest unlocked the wrong room or unpacked a single shirt yet?!
I passed them at the gate two minutes ago asking where to buy noon soup.
Tariq, your eyes are worth their weight in gold—can we move the bags right now?
And leave neat welcome notes on each door table explaining the right hook number!
Grab the master ring, Nour; you take the hatbox, and I have the two backpacks.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (باخد, بياخد).

examples.trans: Someone took my suitcase by mistake!
Old buildings take time to warm up.

meanings.note: First person singular pronoun.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

meanings.note: Conjunction 'or' in statements and open questions.

examples.text: مكتوب عليها اسم أو رقم تليفون؟
examples.trans: Is there a name or phone number written on it?
We need two or three minutes.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite noun أول means 'first' (أول يوم 'first day'); after a definite noun الأول / الأولى agrees in gender (الصفحة الأولى 'the first page'). Also used adverbially ('first').

examples.trans: Welcome on your first day of work!
Read the first page calmly.

meanings.note: Used as a question word or indefinite pronoun.

examples.trans: Which tub of butter did you bring?

examples.text: رني الجرس إذا احتجتي أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.

meanings.note: Warm spoken Levantine affirmation ('yes! / exactly!').

examples.text: أيوا، هاد هو اللحن اللي كنت أدور عليه!
examples.trans: Yes, that's the exact melody I was looking for!

examples.text: أيوا بالزبط، حط الكراسي جنب القوس.
examples.trans: Yes, right there—put the chairs beside the arch.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian pronoun 'you' when addressing one woman.

examples.trans: You must be Nour!
You are today's heroine, Nour.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشتري, بيشتري).

examples.trans: Tell me exactly what to buy.
Buy both brass valves together.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بواب.

examples.trans: The wooden door is open now.
Someone knocked on the door.

meanings.note: Refers to being outdoors or outside a specific location.

examples.trans: It is raining outside.
A yellow taxi stopped outside the gate.

meanings.note: Singular form for any type of card (ID, credit, ticket, etc.).

examples.trans: There is a paper tag on the suitcase.
I wrote my name on the card.

meanings.note: After a plural verb, بعض means 'each other' (بننادي بعض 'we call each other').

examples.trans: We call each other by first name here.

examples.text: ما حكينا مع بعض من زمان.
examples.trans: We have not spoken with each other in a long time.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بوابات.

examples.trans: The courtyard gate is open for guests.
The taxi stopped outside the gate.

meanings.note: Verbal noun of رحّب (to welcome), central to Jordanian hospitality.

examples.trans: The hosts received us with a big welcome.
A short word of welcome makes the guests happy.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بترك, بيترك).

examples.text: مين ترك هاد المغلف جنب الجرس؟
examples.trans: Who left this envelope by the bell?
Thank you for not leaving me in the rain.

meanings.note: Feminine noun from علّق ('to hang'): a wall peg, hook, or hanging tag.

examples.text: المفتاح معلق على أول تعليقة جنب الباب.
examples.trans: The key is hanging on the first hook beside the door.
Put the apron on the hook once you finish.

meanings.note: Form V defective verb from غداء ('lunch'). Past uses -ee- before consonant endings (تغديت).

examples.trans: We are going to have lunch in the garden under the tree.
Did you have lunch or are you still waiting for Tariq?

meanings.note: Everyday masculine noun for a written or official report (تقرير التراث 'the heritage report'). Plural: تقارير.

examples.text: تقرير البلدية مدح ساحتنا يوم الأربعا.
examples.trans: The city report praised our courtyard on Wednesday.

examples.text: كتبت تقرير مختصر عن حالة المبنى.
examples.trans: I wrote a brief report on the condition of the building.

تلخبط.gloss: to get mixed up; get confused

meanings.en: to get mixed up; get confused
meanings.note: Colloquial quadriliteral reflexive verb meaning to become jumbled, tangled, or confused.

examples.text: تلخبطت الأوراق لما فات الهوا من الشباك.
examples.trans: The papers got mixed up when the wind came through the window.

examples.text: ما تتلخبط بالأرقام، اكتبها وحدة وحدة.
examples.trans: Don't get confused with the numbers—write them down one by one.

meanings.note: The number 2.

examples.trans: He has two left on the shelf.
Hold the torch, the two of you!

meanings.note: Extremely common Jordanian expression to express surprise or ask for confirmation, like 'really?' or 'seriously!'.

examples.trans: My grandfather's workshop was on this street.
Did you really finish all the work?

meanings.note: Commonly used preposition for indicating proximity, next to, or beside.

examples.trans: Put a napkin beside every cup.
There is no light beside the bed.

meanings.note: Masculine abstract noun used especially in expressions like لحسن الحظ ('fortunately', literally 'for the goodness of luck').

examples.text: لحسن الحظ لقينا القطار لسه واقف.
examples.trans: Fortunately, we found the train still standing.

examples.text: حسن الضيافة معروف عند أهل البلد.
examples.trans: Goodness of hospitality is well known among the local people.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بحط, بيحط).

examples.trans: Where should I put the spoons and napkins?
I put the suitcase beside the table.

meanings.note: Everyday masculine noun (حظ حلو 'good luck'). Plural: حظوظ.

examples.text: دق الحجرة دقة وحدة عشان الحظ الحلو!
examples.trans: Tap the stone once for good luck!

examples.text: من حسن الحظ لقينا المفتاح بدرج المكتب.
examples.trans: By good luck we found the key in the desk drawer.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to speak, talk, tell' (بحكي / حكى).

examples.trans: Salma chats with all the neighbours.
Tell me everything I need to know.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: حلقات.

examples.trans: The brass ring is twenty millimetres wide.
We fitted a new washer on the pipe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بحمل, بيحمل).

examples.text: بتحمل مفك بكل مكان يا طارق!
examples.trans: You carry a screwdriver everywhere, Tariq!
He picked up the wrong blue bag at the station.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بحجز, بيحجز).

examples.trans: I booked room seven on the phone yesterday.
We booked a quiet dinner at a nearby restaurant.

meanings.note: The number five, used in counting abstractly or before masculine counted nouns.

examples.trans: It is five to twelve.

examples.text: الدكان على بعد خمس دقايق مشي.
examples.trans: The shop is five minutes' walk away.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: دفاتر.

examples.trans: We wrote the name in the booking ledger.
I forgot my leather notebook on the table.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: دقايق.

examples.trans: I will be back in ten minutes on the dot.
Wait one minute, please.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian pronunciation and spelling of ذهب ('gold'). Used both for the metal and a rich golden colour.

examples.trans: The bread came out the colour of gold.
My grandmother has an old gold bracelet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: رئيسية, plural: رئيسيين).

examples.trans: We shut off the main water valve in the cellar.
The main gate is on the quiet street.

meanings.note: Common everyday verb for 'went' in the past tense. Also used as a future particle.

examples.trans: We missed our chance — he hung up!

examples.text: كل التعب راح مع أول فنجان قهوة.
examples.trans: All the tiredness vanished with the first cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Everyday word for a number, digit, or phone number.

examples.trans: Here is your key, room number four.
Is there a phone number written on the paper?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسأل, بيسأل).

examples.trans: Ask him what his name is on the phone!
I came down to ask about the sink water.

meanings.note: Respectful and warm Levantine title for a woman ('Madam / Mrs. / lady').

examples.text: يسلموا إيديكي يا ست سعاد عاللحن الحلو.
examples.trans: Bless your hands, Madam Suad, for the lovely melody.

examples.text: كل ست وشيخ بالحارة معزومين عالافتتاح.
examples.trans: Every lady and elder on the lane is invited to the opening.

meanings.note: The number 6.

examples.trans: Room six is on the second floor.
I have six lemons in the basket.

سلّم.gloss: to greet; say hello; hand over

meanings.en: to greet; say hello; hand over
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسلم, بيسلم).

examples.trans: Give my regards to Salma in the kitchen!
We hand the suitcase over to its owner on Friday.

meanings.note: Spoken defective verb meaning 'to be worth' (يسوى / بتسوى). Distinct from سوّى ('to do/make').

examples.text: الراحة بعد التعب بتسوى الدنيا كلها.
examples.trans: Rest after hard work is worth the whole world.
How much is this rug worth in the market?

meanings.note: Used both as a masculine adjective ('young traveller' مسافر شاب) and a noun ('young man'). Feminine: شابة, plural: شباب.

examples.text: أسبوع شتا حبس مسافر شاب هون.
examples.trans: A rainy week trapped a young traveller here.
The young people helped carry the chairs to the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Form I transitive verb taking the thing resembled directly without a preposition.

examples.trans: This cup looks like my grandmother's cup.
The two boys resemble each other in their laugh.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشرح, بيشرح).

examples.trans: Explain the story to him in your calm voice.
He explained the legal clause to us simply.

meanings.note: Universal Jordanian/Levantine word (from Turkish çanta) for any handbag, backpack, or travel suitcase.

examples.trans: This blue suitcase is very heavy.
We set the suitcases beside the reception desk.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: شوربات.

examples.trans: Here is a cup of hot vegetable soup.
Hot soup is wonderful on a rainy day.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بصير, بيصير).

examples.trans: You became one of us quickly!
Did the water upstairs turn cold?

meanings.note: Everyday word confirming something is right ('right! / true!').

examples.text: صح! في صفحة تانية ورا الرسالة.
examples.trans: Right! There is a second page behind the letter.
What you say is completely true.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian spelling/pronunciation (duhur) for midday (12:00 p.m.).

examples.text: الكافيه بيقدم شوربة سخنة من الضهر للمسا.
examples.trans: The café serves hot soup from noon until evening.

examples.text: الشمس بتكون عالية ودافية وقت الضهر.
examples.trans: The sun is high and warm at noon.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun (feminine: ضيفة). Plural: ضيوف.

examples.trans: The guests are coming down to breakfast now.
We welcomed every guest with a smile.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: طوابق.

examples.trans: Your room is on the second floor on the right.
The building has three storeys.

meanings.note: Common everyday word for table.

examples.trans: We set four tables in the courtyard.
Breakfast is ready on the table.

meanings.note: Form II طلّع means both 'look!' (طلّع بالمراية) and 'bring/carry up' (رح أطلّع الشنتة).

examples.text: طلع بالمراية ورا المكتب يا معلم!
examples.trans: Look in the mirror behind the desk, boss!
I will carry the blue suitcase up for you.

meanings.note: Can refer to a cardboard box, a tin can, or a small container.

examples.trans: The gold tin is on the top shelf.
I saved this old wooden box.

meanings.note: Standard preposition for 'on', 'upon', or 'to'.

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Means 'about' (عن الزبدة), 'off / away from' (عن جبيني), and appears in عن جد ('really!') and عن إذنك ('excuse me').

examples.trans: I will carry the suitcase up for you.
I heard your voices about the butter!

meanings.note: Feminine noun; also used in the delighted Jordanian exclamation يا عيني! ('oh my! / how lovely!').

examples.trans: Close your eyes and smell the coffee!
Oh my, look at that warm light in the courtyard!

meanings.note: Colloquial Levantine noun describing hazy vision, mist, or blurred ink.

examples.text: الدنيا الصبح كانت كلها غباش من الضباب.
examples.trans: Everything this morning was blurry with fog.

examples.text: لو في غباش بالعدسة، امسحها بمنديل ناعم.
examples.trans: If there is haze on the lens, wipe it with a soft cloth.

meanings.note: Masculine noun whose plural أغراض ('things, belongings, groceries') is one of the commonest words in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Put your things in the cupboard beside the door.
I have a quick errand in the market and I'll be back.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for a room in a house or building.

examples.trans: We have eight comfortable rooms at the guesthouse.
Room four is ready and clean.

meanings.note: Used as noun in بالغلط ('by mistake') and عالغلط ('for the mistake'), and invariable predicate 'wrong' (في شي غلط something is wrong).

examples.trans: He took the other suitcase by mistake.
Sorry for the mistake, my apologies.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفتح, بيفتح).

examples.trans: The corner shop opens at seven.
Oh, the door finally opened!

meanings.note: Adverb 'right away, at once'.

examples.trans: Count on me, I am heading out right away!
The hot water came back immediately.

meanings.note: Feminine noun for a brimmed sun hat, straw hat, or cap.

examples.text: البس قبعة قش لما تمشي بالشمس.
examples.trans: Wear a straw hat when you walk in the sun.
Her floral hat is hanging on the door.

meanings.note: Preposition and adverb for time or sequence meaning 'prior to' or 'before'.

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقدر, بيقدر).

examples.text: بنقدر نقدم زبدة مالحة مع المربى؟
examples.trans: Can we serve salted butter with jam?

examples.text: ليش ما قدرت تعطيه القطار بإيدك؟
examples.trans: Why could you not hand him the train yourself?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for soon or near.

examples.text: علمت بيانو ببيت قريب من هون.
examples.trans: I taught piano in a house near here.
We booked a table at a nearby restaurant.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: قمصان.

examples.trans: He put on a neat, ironed white shirt.
He changed his shirt twice before the appointment.

meanings.note: Past tense of 'to be' for 3rd person masculine singular. Widely used as an auxiliary verb.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day will not be boring!

meanings.note: A highly versatile quantifier used to mean 'all of', 'every', or 'the whole'.

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'no' or 'not', used exactly like Standard Arabic.

examples.trans: No, lift the handle first.
Do not worry, ma'am.

meanings.note: Very common Jordanian word to indicate that an action is ongoing or hasn't happened yet.

examples.trans: Is your cup still intact?
Nobody has written anything yet.

meanings.note: Also used in the mild Jordanian exclamation يا لطيف! ('goodness gracious!').

examples.trans: Hot bread makes people pleasant!
Goodness gracious, the suitcase is so heavy!

meanings.note: Common conjunction used to introduce a time clause, distinct from the question word 'when' (mita).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
When I get nervous, my sentences turn long.

meanings.note: Form II passive participle from أدب ('manners'): describes courteous speech or polite people.

examples.trans: The new students are very polite and kind.

examples.text: بنت صغيرة مؤدبة فتحت النا الباب.
examples.trans: A polite little girl opened the door for us.

meanings.note: Form V active participle from جال ('to roam'), used as a noun for hikers, walkers, or strolling visitors.

examples.trans: The hikers reached the mountain before sunset.
There is a trail set aside for hikers in the forest.

meanings.note: Used to describe a neat person, a well-organized room, or generally something of high quality (e.g. 'a nice car').

examples.trans: I recognized your neat handwriting right away.
Neat pencil sketches.

مرق.gloss: to pass by; walk past; drop by

meanings.en: to pass by; walk past; drop by
meanings.note: Quintessential Levantine verb for walking past a street or dropping by.

examples.text: أي حدا بيمرق من شارع الرينبو بيقرأ اللوحة بوضوح.
examples.trans: Anyone walking down Rainbow Street can read the sign clearly.

examples.text: مرق جارنا الساعاتي الصبح وسلم علينا.
examples.trans: Our watchmaker neighbour dropped by in the morning and said hello.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: In Jordanian speech, يا معلم is an affectionate, respectful way to address a boss or skilled craftsperson.

examples.trans: You are all generosity, boss!
She was a very gifted piano teacher.

meanings.note: Means both a door key and a mechanic's spanner/wrench (مفتاح حديد iron wrench).

examples.trans: Here is the key to room four.
We have eight brass keys on the board.

meanings.note: Form I passive participle from قلب ('to flip'). With بـ, بالمقلوب means 'upside down / backwards'.

examples.trans: The sign is hung upside down on the door!

examples.text: الورقة مقلوبة، لفها عشان تقرأ المكتوب.
examples.trans: The sheet is upside down—turn it round to read what's written.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مكالمات.

examples.trans: An important phone call came in on the landline.
She finished the call in two minutes.

meanings.note: One of the most basic Arabic prepositions indicating origin.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Form II passive participle from ورد ('rose/flower'): describes floral fabric or patterns.

examples.trans: She put a floral shawl over her shoulders.
The floral curtain brightened up the room.

meanings.note: Singular نظارة means one pair of glasses in Arabic (نظارتي my glasses); dual نظارتين means two pairs of glasses!

examples.trans: I cannot find my glasses on the desk!
He pulled his glasses down off his forehead and laughed.

meanings.note: Vocalized lemma distinguishing the verb 'to move/relocate' from the noun نقل ('transport').

examples.trans: We moved the piano to the dry corner of the room.

examples.text: نور نقلت المواعيد من الدفتر للوح الأبيض.
examples.trans: Nour copied the dates from the notebook onto the whiteboard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنزل, بينزل).

examples.trans: The guests will come down at half past seven.
I came down to ask about the sink water.

meanings.note: Masculine هادي ('quiet') is homographic with the feminine demonstrative هادي ('this'); context and agreement distinguish them cleanly.

examples.trans: The spot above the tree is very quiet.
We prepared the quiet attic room for you.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'now / right now' (pronounced halla' in Amman).

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door now.
We will check the tag right now.

meanings.note: Cardinal number or used as an indefinite pronoun.

examples.trans: Not a single scratch on the cup!
The gate rang with one strong ring.

meanings.note: Collective noun used for paper material or leaves of a tree.

examples.trans: We use a paper ledger and a pencil.
He wrote a note on a small slip of paper.

meanings.note: Used for physical weight on a foot, scale measurements, or poetic meter.

examples.text: لا تحطي أي وزن عكاحلك اليوم أبدا.
examples.trans: Don't put any weight on your ankle at all today.

examples.text: قيس وزن الطحين والسكر بالميزان قبل العجن.
examples.trans: Weigh the flour and sugar on the scale before kneading.

meanings.note: General term for time or duration.

examples.trans: Old pipes take time to warm up.
You arrived right on time.

meanings.note: Used in negative constructions or as a strong negative emphasis.

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Appears in the dramatic warning يا ويل البنت اللي... ('woe to the girl who... / heaven help the girl who...').

examples.text: يا ويل اللي بيتأخر عن الحصة.
examples.trans: Woe to whoever is late to class.
We're in trouble if the teacher heard us.

meanings.note: The standard interrogative adverb for location in the dialect.

examples.trans: Where is the computer, Tariq?
Where should I put the small spoons?

meanings.note: Vocative particle used when addressing someone directly.

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Everyday conversational bridge introducing an inference ('so that means...'), clarification, or gentle pause ('I mean...').

examples.trans: So the house says hello by itself?
Does that mean there is no heating tonight?
